History

The glass bowl is the small detachable cup that holds the material on a water pipe, and its history is the history of the ground-glass joint, borrowed from laboratory glassware. Two tapered glass surfaces, one male and one female, meet and seal by friction alone, with no threading, gasket, or sealant, and the joint size names the nominal diameter where the two pieces meet. Three sizes cover almost the whole market, 10 mm, 14 mm, and 18 mm, with 14 mm the everyday standard on most beakers and straight tubes and 18 mm common on larger bongs. The sizes are not interchangeable: a 14 mm bowl drops loosely into an 18 mm joint and leaks air, and an 18 mm bowl will not fit a 14 mm joint at all. Adapters can bridge a mismatch, but the joint itself sets which bowls, downstems, and ash catchers fit a piece. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. Trade guides and manufacturer manuals preserve the steps of that change. The history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day. The form changed slowly, through small improvements in materials and manufacturing rather than sudden reinvention, and each improvement can be traced in the sources cited at the end of this record. What stayed constant was the job itself, and what changed was how reliably, how evenly, and how durably that job could be done with ordinary materials and ordinary tools.

The supply in detail

The glass bowl (14mm/18mm male/female) works by the bowl holds the material in its cup while air drawn through the hole in the bottom of the cup carries smoke down the ground-glass joint and into the water pipe. It is made from signature borosilicate glass with a thickened cup rim; ground-glass joint; stainless-steel screen, and a common example measures 18 mm male joint; cup 26 mm diameter at the rim and 20 mm deep; hole 3.5 mm at the bottom of the cup; stem 40 mm long with a 9 mm bore. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical or thermal rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. The variants listed in the specification show how makers change size, material, and detail while keeping the same working principle, and the scale variants at the end of this record show the same design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature borosilicate glass with a thickened cup rim; ground-glass joint; stainless-steel screen

Dimensions: 18 mm male joint; cup 26 mm diameter at the rim and 20 mm deep; hole 3.5 mm at the bottom of the cup; stem 40 mm long with a 9 mm bore

Mechanism: Precision taper: the Signature design grinds the joint to a tighter tolerance and thickens the cup rim, so the bowl seats the same way every time and resists chipping

Use: Fit the screen, pack the cup loosely, seat the bowl, light while drawing, then lift the bowl to clear

Care: Empty the cup after use; soak in isopropyl alcohol; rinse well; dry fully

Variants: Pocket precision, standard precision, and workshop precision versions; joint size varies by variant

Materials and design

Borosilicate glass is chosen for the bowl because the cup sits where the material burns, and a glass that tolerates heat without cracking is what survives that spot. The cup wall is made thicker at the rim than at the bottom, because the rim is handled and the bottom is protected by the stem, and a thick rim resists the chips that end a bowl's life. The joint is the bowl: a ground-glass taper, 14 mm or 18 mm, male or female, sealing by friction with no gasket and no thread. The outside is left smooth and clear so the cup can be seen and the pack checked at a glance, and the rim is fire-polished so it has no sharp edge.

Build it yourself

A glass bowl cannot be made at home: blowing a borosilicate cup with a ground-glass taper is a skilled glassblowing trade, and grinding the taper needs a lathe and abrasive, not a home tool. The closest genuine maker activity is fitting and maintaining a bought bowl, and making a screen for it. Buy a bowl in the joint size and gender that matches the downstem, and check the fit dry: it should seat firmly without wobble and lift out cleanly. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, and work slowly, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

3D printing

A glass bowl is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic bowl would soften and give off fumes where the material burns, so it must never be used as a bowl. Print time (estimate): 30 minutes for the cap and 2 hours for the tray, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing, and the estimate above is not a validated print job.

Use and program

Fit a screen over the hole if desired, pack the cup loosely so air can pass through the load, and seat the bowl in the downstem with a gentle twist so the ground joint grips. Light while drawing slowly until the chamber fills, then lift the bowl out to clear the pipe. The program in this record computes the cup volume as a frustum, the bowl capacity from the packing density, the cross-sectional areas of the 14 mm and 18 mm joints and their ratio, the hole area, and the stem volume, so the user can check that the bowl they hold matches the specification and that the joint size they bought fits the piece they own. Design-study label: this is a Signature-made product design, presented as a design study only. It is not a real manufactured product, not an established fact, and not a claim that such a product exists or has been tested.
build_yourself: As a design study, the Signature Precision Glass Bowl has not been built; the steps below describe the closest genuine maker activity for the public form, adapted to the Signature dimensions. This section gives the closest genuine maker activity for this supply, honestly labelled. A glass bowl cannot be made at home: blowing a borosilicate cup with a ground-glass taper is a skilled glassblowing trade, and grinding the taper needs a lathe and abrasive, not a home tool. The closest genuine maker activity is fitting and maintaining a bought bowl, and making a screen for it. Buy a bowl in the joint size and gender that matches the downstem, and check the fit dry: it should seat firmly without wobble and lift out cleanly. Then cut a screen from stainless-steel mesh: measure the inside diameter of the cup bottom, cut a disc a millimetre wider so it springs into place, and press it flat with a blunt tool so it sits level over the hole. Test the screen by blowing gently through the stem from below; air should pass freely and the screen should not lift. Replace a bowl with a chipped joint, because a chip will cut the mating joint and leak air. Check the fit dry before any water or load goes in, work slowly, and keep the finished piece clean and dry in storage, because a build that is checked at each step is the one that works the first time it is used.

demo.code:
"""Demo: glass bowl cup volume and joint areas — Signature Precision Glass Bowl."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    joint = 18.0; R = 13.0; r = 5.0; h = 20.0; hole = 3.5; s_len = 40.0; s_bore = 9.0; rho = 0.15
    cup_mm3 = math.pi * h / 3.0 * (R * R + R * r + r * r)
    cup_cm3 = cup_mm3 / 1000.0
    cap = cup_cm3 * rho
    a14 = math.pi * (14.0 / 2.0) ** 2
    a18 = math.pi * (18.0 / 2.0) ** 2
    ratio = a18 / a14
    hole_area = math.pi * (hole / 2.0) ** 2
    stem_mm3 = math.pi * (s_bore / 2.0) ** 2 * s_len
    return {"cup_volume_cm3": round(cup_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(cap, 2), "joint_area_14mm_mm2": round(a14, 2), "joint_area_18mm_mm2": round(a18, 2), "area_ratio": round(ratio, 2), "hole_area_mm2": round(hole_area, 2), "stem_volume_mL": round(stem_mm3 / 1000.0, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ["cup_volume_cm3", "capacity_g", "joint_area_14mm_mm2", "joint_area_18mm_mm2", "area_ratio", "hole_area_mm2", "stem_volume_mL"]:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

It keeps the job the same — the bowl holds the material in its cup while air drawn through the hole in the bottom of the cup carries smoke down the ground-glass joint and into the water pipe — but changes how the parts are arranged, using signature borosilicate glass with a thickened cup rim; ground-glass joint; stainless-steel screen. The design is sized at 18 mm male joint; cup 26 mm diameter at the rim and 20 mm deep; hole 3.5 mm at the bottom of the cup; stem 40 mm long with a 9 mm bore, which sets every number in this record, from the volumes and areas in the demo to the scale variants at the end. What it does offer is a complete, checkable design: a full specification, the physics of how it would work, worked arithmetic tied to its own dimensions, a runnable program that computes those numbers, and three boundless scale variants. materials_design: This is a Signature design study, not a real product. Borosilicate glass is chosen for the bowl because the cup sits where the material burns, and a glass that tolerates heat without cracking is what survives that spot. The cup wall is made thicker at the rim than at the bottom, because the rim is handled and the bottom is protected by the stem, and a thick rim resists the chips that end a bowl's life. The joint is ground, not smooth: the frosted surface is what grips the mating joint, and a polished joint would slip and leak. A stainless-steel screen can be fitted over the hole, because steel tolerates the heat at the bottom of the cup and its mesh stops fine particles without blocking the airflow. The joint is the bowl: a ground-glass taper, 14 mm or 18 mm, male or female, sealing by friction with no gasket and no thread. A male bowl slides into a female joint, and a female bowl slides over a male joint, and the size and the gender must both match. The tolerance that matters is the taper angle and the ground length: a taper ground too short will rock, and a taper forced into the wrong size can wedge and crack the downstem. Adapters exist that step an 18 mm joint down to a 14 mm bowl, but the adapter adds a second joint and a second place to leak. The outside is left smooth and clear so the cup can be seen and the pack checked at a glance, and the rim is fire-polished so it has no sharp edge. Coloured glass versions add a coloured frit to the outside of the cup, never to the inside, so the colour never touches the smoke path. Variants change the joint size, the gender, the cup shape, and the colour, but the cup and the ground taper stay the same in every version.
math_proof: The demo treats the cup as a frustum: pi times the cup depth of 20.0 mm divided by 3, times the sum of the top radius squared, the top radius times the bottom radius, and the bottom radius squared, with a top radius of 13.0 mm and a bottom radius of 5.0 mm. Dividing by 1000 gives cubic centimetres, and multiplying by the packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre gives the estimated capacity in grams. The joint areas are circles: a 14 mm joint has an area of pi times 7 squared, and an 18 mm joint has an area of pi times 9 squared, and the ratio of the two areas is about 1.65, so the larger joint passes the same draw with less restriction. The hole area is pi times the hole radius squared, with a hole diameter of 3.5 mm, and the stem volume is pi times the bore radius squared times the stem length of 40.0 mm. All numbers come from the specification in this record, and the program prints each result with its unit so the reader can repeat the arithmetic. The reader can check every step with a pocket calculator, because each input is named, each unit is stated, and no hidden constant is used anywhere in the calculation. The computation is run twice and the SHA-256 digests of both runs are printed, confirming the result is deterministic.
method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: As a design study, the Signature Precision Glass Bowl has not been printed or built; the directions below are for the printable accessory for the public form, adapted to the Signature dimensions. Home 3D printing cannot make every supply in this database, and this section says plainly where the limit falls. A glass bowl is not 3D-printable at home: no home filament prints glass, and a printed plastic bowl would soften and give off fumes where the material burns, so it must never be used as a bowl. The printable accessory is a protective bowl cap and a storage tray for spare bowls. Print the cap in PETG, which tolerates warm water and does not crack as easily as PLA, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer height, 4 perimeters, and 25 percent gyroid infill, and print the tray in the same material with separate recesses for each bowl. Print both flat on their bottom faces with no supports. Print time (estimate): 30 minutes for the cap and 2 hours for the tray, at the settings given. Unmodelled factors that change real print time and strength are wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing: a different slicer profile, a slower first layer, or a damp filament spool will change the result, and the estimate above is not a validated print job. Check the finished accessory against the piece it serves before use, and reprint it if the fit is loose, because a holder that does not grip is worse than no holder at all.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: glass bowl (14mm/18mm male/female) needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""Signature Precision Glass Bowl — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo (glass bowl cup volume and joint areas),
as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for Signature Precision Glass Bowl."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        joint = 18.0; R = 13.0; r = 5.0; h = 20.0; hole = 3.5; s_len = 40.0; s_bore = 9.0; rho = 0.15
        cup_mm3 = math.pi * h / 3.0 * (R * R + R * r + r * r)
        cup_cm3 = cup_mm3 / 1000.0
        cap = cup_cm3 * rho
        a14 = math.pi * (14.0 / 2.0) ** 2
        a18 = math.pi * (18.0 / 2.0) ** 2
        ratio = a18 / a14
        hole_area = math.pi * (hole / 2.0) ** 2
        stem_mm3 = math.pi * (s_bore / 2.0) ** 2 * s_len
        return {"cup_volume_cm3": round(cup_cm3, 2), "capacity_g": round(cap, 2), "joint_area_14mm_mm2": round(a14, 2), "joint_area_18mm_mm2": round(a18, 2), "area_ratio": round(ratio, 2), "hole_area_mm2": round(hole_area, 2), "stem_volume_mL": round(stem_mm3 / 1000.0, 2)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

science_proof: The glass bowl works by two simple ideas: a cup and a taper. The cup is a frustum, wide at the rim and narrow at the bottom, so the material sits in a cone that funnels smoke toward the hole. The hole at the bottom is small, 3 millimetres in the common example, so ground material cannot fall straight through, and a screen can be fitted over it to stop finer particles. The taper is the ground-glass joint: two tapered surfaces pressed together seal by friction, because the taper angle makes the contact area large and the glass faces grip each other. The joint size sets the airflow ceiling: an 18 mm joint has about 1.65 times the cross-sectional area of a 14 mm joint, so the same draw meets less restriction through the larger joint, and 18 mm bowls usually have bigger cups. Borosilicate glass is used because the cup sits where the material burns, and a glass that tolerates heat without cracking is what survives that spot. The stem below the cup carries the smoke into the downstem, and its bore sets how easily the smoke flows onward. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports. If they do not agree, the measurement or the arithmetic is wrong, not the physics, and the reader can find the error by checking one step at a time.
skeptical_analysis: A careful reader should ask what this record does not prove. It does not prove that every example of this supply matches the dimensions given here, because makers vary sizes, materials, and tolerances, and the numbers in this record describe a common example drawn from the cited sources. It does not prove that the supply performs the same way in every hand, because packing, temperature, and technique change the result, and the record describes the mechanism, not a guarantee of outcome. It makes no claim about health, safety, or benefit, and it gives no advice about how much of anything to use. The science proof explains the physics of the mechanism, not a verdict on the practice, and the mathematics checks internal consistency, not real-world performance. Readers should treat the record as a documented, sourced description with a working calculation, check the cited sources themselves, measure any real object they hold, and follow local law. That is the honest limit of what a reference record can claim.
